Well, that is the central tragedy of this entire conflict, isn't it? The truth is, the international community has largely drawn back from intervening in a way that could halt the bloodshed. We would likely see immediate border closures within the Schengen area, intense political panic in capitals like Berlin and Brussels, and a frantic scramble to renegotiate financial aid or diplomatic terms with Ankara. It’s classic brinksmanship. Turkey feels like it’s bearing an unfair burden alone and not getting enough genuine support or backing from the West for its security zones or its policies in northern Syria. So using refugees as leverage is a powerful and desperate tool to force Europe and NATO to pay attention and give them what they want. But the human cost would be catastrophic for the refugees caught in the middle of this geopolitical game.

When you talk to everyday Afghans, the overriding desire is just for the fighting to stop so they can rebuild their lives and provide for their families. While there are profound concerns about what any political settlement means for governance, human rights, and the future of the country, the sheer exhaustion with conflict drives this sentiment. At the same time, any lasting outcome has to ensure that the hard-fought gains of the last twenty years—particularly for women and civil society—aren't completely erased. The challenge ahead will be whether a negotiated settlement can genuinely protect those interests while bringing a real end to the violence.

Look, after decades of relentless conflict, the psychological and physical toll on the Afghan people is almost impossible to overstate. Every family has suffered profound loss. When you speak with ordinary citizens across the country, a clear consensus emerges: safety, survival, and an end to the daily violence take absolute precedence over everything else. People are simply exhausted. 

While there are deeply justified fears about what a negotiated settlement might mean for human rights, civil society, and governance—particularly for women and minorities—the overwhelming sentiment is that the status quo is entirely unsustainable. If a political accommodation with the Taliban is the only viable path to stop the bloodshed and bring a measure of stability, many Afghans are prepared to accept deeply painful compromises. They have reached a breaking point where peace, even an imperfect one, is the ultimate necessity.

We are exhausted. For forty years, my people have known nothing but war, blood, and displacement. Every single family has lost someone. When you live in perpetual fear of a bomb dropping or a gun battle in your street, your perspective shifts entirely. We are not asking for an ideal government anymore; we are just asking to survive. If a compromise brings an end to the killing, if it means our children can walk to school without terror, then we must accept it. Pride and political ideals will not feed our families or heal our wounds. Peace is the only victory left available to us, and we are ready to take it, whatever the cost.

Look, the reality on the ground is stark. Afghans are exhausted by decades of relentless war, displacement, and economic devastation. When you talk to people in the markets of Kabul or the provinces, their primary concern is no longer the ideological purity of the government or the geopolitical strategy of the West; it is simply physical survival and the end of the bloodshed. If a political settlement requires bringing the Taliban into a power-sharing arrangement or making painful compromises, a vast number of citizens are prepared to accept that grim bargain because the alternative—endless, grinding conflict—is simply no longer tolerable. They want the killing to stop, and they are willing to risk an uncertain peace over a certain, unending war.

Look, the reality on the ground in Afghanistan is sobering, and we have to be honest about our limits. After nearly two decades of war and immense expenditures of blood and treasure, we have to recognize that a permanent military footprint is neither sustainable nor necessary for our core security. Afghans themselves are weary and desperate for an end to the fighting, and if that requires a political settlement—even one involving difficult compromises with the Taliban—that is ultimately a choice for them to make. Our grand ambitions of nation-building were never realistic, and it is past time for us to bring our troops home, rely on our vast strategic cushion, and focus our resources on domestic priorities here at home rather than trying to police every conflict across the globe.

Well, I think any political resolution to the conflict in Afghanistan ultimately has to be led and owned by Afghans themselves. From our perspective at USAID and across the government, the focus is on supporting a stable, representative government that can provide for its people and ensure the country never again becomes a safe haven for international terrorism. Any process of reconciliation or reintegration has to involve Afghans deciding the terms of their own future, ensuring that the constitutional gains made over the last decade, particularly regarding the rights of women and minorities, are protected. Our job is to help build the institutional capacity and economic foundation so that whatever political arrangements emerge, the Afghan state has the resilience to stand on its own feet and deliver basic services to its citizens.

That is the million-dollar question, isn't it? Ultimately, any sustainable resolution to the conflict in Afghanistan has to be political, not purely military. But when we talk about reintegration and reconciliation, there are strict conditions that the international community and the Afghan government have to maintain. Any outcome must preserve the constitutional gains of the last decade, particularly regarding the rights of women, human rights, and the rule of law. So while engagement and eventual political settlement with elements who are willing to lay down arms, cut ties with al-Qaeda, and accept the constitution are necessary components of a long-term strategy, it cannot simply be a wholesale handover or a compromise of those fundamental values. It has to be a process led by Afghans that protects the future of their democracy and security.

That is certainly one facet of what a comprehensive political settlement would entail, but I think we are getting ahead of ourselves. The fundamental reality on the ground is that there is no purely military solution to this conflict. We have maintained for years that an inclusive, Afghan-led and Afghan-owned process is the only path to lasting stability. Any sustainable peace will require all factions, including the Taliban, to engage in serious negotiations regarding governance, constitutional rights, and the rule of law. Our primary objective remains ensuring that Afghanistan never again serves as a safe haven for international terrorism, and we must pursue every diplomatic avenue to achieve that while supporting the Afghan security forces and civil society.

Look, it means recognizing the reality on the ground that there is no purely military solution to this conflict. When we talk about a political settlement, it has to be inclusive of all major Afghan stakeholders, and yes, that includes the Taliban, but it has to be done in a way that preserves the constitutional gains, the rights of women and minorities, and the democratic institutions that the Afghan people and the international community have invested so heavily in over the last two decades. It is not about simply handing over power, but rather finding a negotiated framework where they participate in governance under the rule of law, subject to international standards and continued oversight, because the alternative is endless civil war.

Well, I think sooner or later, any realistic assessment of the situation in Afghanistan has to recognize that a purely military victory isn't in the cards. We've been there for a decade, and if we're going to stabilize the country and eventually bring our troops home, there has to be some sort of political settlement involving the major domestic factions. That doesn't mean we endorse their worldview, but it does mean acknowledging the political reality on the ground. We have to be much smarter about our priorities and where we invest our resources, rather than getting bogged down indefinitely in conflicts that don't directly threaten our core national security.

Well, the prospects for peace are undeniably complicated and fraught with challenges, as they have been for years. When we helped draft the constitution and build the framework for a modern Afghan state, the goal was always to create an inclusive system where grievances could be addressed through political channels rather than violence. The Taliban’s persistent refusal to engage directly with the Afghan government is a major obstacle, because a sustainable peace ultimately requires an Afghan-led and Afghan-owned political settlement. 

However, engagement remains essential. We have to continue supporting the institutional capacity of the Afghan government so that it remains a credible, viable partner for its own people and for the international community. If the government can demonstrate effective governance, deliver services, and maintain the support of its populace, that changes the dynamic. Peace won't happen overnight, but there is no military-only solution. It has to come through eventual political accommodation backed by resolute international support.

Well, it's a very sobering reality. The Taliban's reluctance to engage directly with the Afghan government remains one of the most formidable obstacles to a sustainable peace. For a long time, the hope was that economic development, institutional building, and the creation of a constitutional framework would provide the strong foundation needed for Afghans to resolve their own differences. But peace isn't just about treaties or political architecture; it requires a genuine willingness from all sides to accept a shared future under the rule of law. If the Taliban refuses to recognize the legitimacy of the state and engage in serious, good-faith dialogue, the prospects for a lasting, stable peace become exceedingly difficult. Ultimately, any durable solution has to be led by Afghans themselves, protecting the hard-won gains in governance, rights, and development that have been achieved over the past two decades.

Well, it is a formidable challenge, but I remain convinced that a sustainable peace cannot be achieved by bypassing the legitimate institutions of the Afghan state. The constitution we helped draft enshrined fundamental rights—for women, minorities, and civil society—that simply cannot be bargained away for a fragile, expedient ceasefire. The Taliban must recognize that legitimacy comes from the Afghan people, not the barrel of a gun. If the international community maintains its resolve and insists that any political settlement includes the preservation of the republic's democratic framework, there is still a pathway forward. It requires immense patience, unwavering diplomatic pressure, and the steadfast refusal to abandon those who have fought so hard for a pluralistic future.

It is a very daunting picture, but I don’t think it’s hopeless. The Taliban’s refusal to talk directly to the Afghan government has been the major stumbling block, but we have to look past the official rhetoric. There are private conversations happening, and there is a growing realization on all sides that a military stalemate cannot be sustained forever. The key is regional diplomacy—bringing in neighbors who also have a vital interest in a stable Afghanistan rather than a collapsed state. We also have to ensure that the monumental social and democratic gains of the last two decades, especially regarding women and minorities, are not bargained away in the dark. Peace is only possible if it is an Afghan-led process that preserves the republic, protects the constitution, and offers the Taliban a political pathway forward that doesn't involve subjugating the entire population.

Well, I think we have to be realistic about what can be achieved through a negotiated settlement. After decades of conflict, the idea that we are going to achieve some sort of neat, total victory or establish a stable, centralized democracy that can permanently exclude the Taliban is simply not supported by the facts on the ground. The United States has spent immense resources and time trying to reshape Afghanistan, but local forces and entrenched political realities always reassert themselves. 

If there is to be peace, it will likely involve some form of power-sharing or accommodation that reflects the actual balance of power, rather than the outcome we might ideally wish for. Our priority should be recognizing the limits of our influence and ensuring we do not remain indefinitely trapped in a conflict that no longer serves our core national security interests.

Well, I think it's very early to predict the precise shape of any future negotiations, but the Afghan government has consistently stated that any process must be led by Afghans themselves and must adhere to certain fundamental principles. That means participants would need to respect the Afghan constitution, renounce violence, and cut ties with international terrorist groups like al-Qaida. From our perspective at USAID and across the administration, the primary focus remains supporting the civilian institutions and the economic stability that will allow the Afghan state to stand on its own feet. Whether and how reconciliation unfolds will ultimately depend on the political choices made by Afghans, but our long-term commitment is to ensure that the country doesn't slide backward into chaos and that the development gains achieved over the last decade are protected.

Well, I think any credible negotiation process has to be led and owned by Afghans themselves, grounded in the realities of the constitution and the progress that has been made over the last decade and a half, particularly regarding the rights of women and civil society. It cannot simply be a power-sharing arrangement among elites at the expense of the broader population. At the same time, we know from history and from our development work on the ground that sustainable peace requires addressing the underlying drivers of conflict, providing economic opportunities, and ensuring that regional actors play a constructive role rather than a spoiler one. It's an immensely complicated path, and while the international community can support and facilitate dialogue, the hard choices about governance, integration, and reconciliation ultimately rest with the Afghan people and their leadership.

Well, look, if and when these talks actually happen, they have to be led and owned by Afghans themselves, but the shape of them is going to be incredibly complex. From what we are hearing, the framework would likely start with confidence-building measures, maybe addressing a reduction in violence or a ceasefire, before moving into the core constitutional and political issues. The Taliban are going to come to the table demanding a very specific interpretation of Islamic law and a complete restructuring of the current political system, while the republic's representatives are deeply committed to preserving the democratic gains, women's rights, and the constitution of the last two decades. So it won't be a single sit-down, but rather a long, grueling process of phased bargaining, heavily reliant on regional and international guarantors to keep both sides engaged and moving forward.

Well, it’s early, but I think we can outline the contours of what those talks would have to entail. First, they have to be Afghan-led and Afghan-owned, which is a cliché, but it’s fundamentally true—outsiders cannot dictate the terms of coexistence for them. What it likely looks like is a very painful, protracted bargaining process where the Taliban are forced to test whether they can achieve their goals through politics rather than violence, while the Republic forces must figure out how to preserve the constitutional gains of the last two decades, particularly regarding women’s rights and minority protections. It won't be a neat or quick peace agreement; it will likely be a phased arrangement, perhaps starting with a reduction of violence, leading to a ceasefire, and then grinding through the existential questions of power-sharing and the future governance of the state.

Well, if negotiations ever truly get off the ground, they are bound to be extremely protracted and difficult, because the fundamental goals of the two sides are largely incompatible. The Taliban are going to want to regain a significant share of power and roll back many of the social and political changes of the last decade, particularly regarding women's rights and governance. On the other hand, the current Afghan government and civil society elements will resist that. But the hard reality is that after years of fighting, there is no military solution to this conflict. At some point, a political settlement is the only way out. The United States has recognized this, which is why there's been talk of a diplomatic track, but managing expectations and recognizing that any resulting settlement may not look like a neat, western-style democracy is going to be essential.

Well, I think the history of these negotiations shows that you rarely get a clean, sequential process where you achieve a total cease-fire first and then neatly move into political discussions. More often, the two things have to happen in tandem. You need enough of a reduction in violence to create the breathing room and the security required for leaders to sit down and make difficult political compromises. At the same time, without a credible political horizon, without a sense of where this process is actually leading for all sides, it is very difficult to sustain any cessation of hostilities on the ground. So it is less about which comes first in absolute terms, and more about how progress on one track reinforces and unlocks progress on the other, even when it is messy and difficult.

Well, I think the history of these negotiations suggests that you cannot easily separate the two, because a cease-fire without a clear political pathway forward is rarely sustainable. When parties stop fighting, they need to believe that the political process will address their core grievances and aspirations. At the same time, negotiating under the constant pressure of active conflict makes it exceedingly difficult to build the trust necessary for a lasting political settlement. So the international community and the local leadership usually have to work on both tracks simultaneously—using a reduction in violence to create the breathing room required for serious political compromise, while recognizing that the ultimate security of any cease-fire depends entirely on the credibility of the political deal that follows.

Well, look, history shows us that you can't decouple the security track from the political horizon. If you just agree to a temporary cessation of hostilities without addressing the underlying drivers of the conflict—the occupation, the blockades, the fundamental lack of sovereignty and security for both peoples—you're just hitting the pause button on a tragedy. We have seen this movie before. The shooting stops, everyone catches their breath, and then the violence erupts again because the root causes remain festering. So the sequence has to be integrated. You need a credible, binding political framework that guarantees self-determination and safety, and the cessation of violence must serve that ultimate goal. Otherwise, a cease-fire is just an illusion that paves the way for the next war, and neither Israelis nor Palestinians can afford another cycle of bloodshed.

Look, history and every serious mediator will tell you that trying to sequence a permanent political settlement while bullets are flying is a recipe for failure. You cannot negotiate a viable future for governance, borders, and rights under intense bombardment. You need an immediate, durable cessation of hostilities to create the basic human security and psychological space required for leaders to even contemplate hard compromises. At the same time, a pure pause without a clear, enforced political horizon just leads right back to war. So the cessation of violence has to come first to stop the bleeding, but it must be explicitly tethered from day one to a credible political framework. Otherwise, you are just pressing a pause button on a catastrophe.

Well, I think history suggests that trying to resolve all the underlying political disputes before securing a cease-fire is usually a recipe for endless fighting. You almost always need at least a provisional cessation of hostilities—a way to stop the bleeding—before the parties are ever going to sit down and negotiate in good faith over the long-term political architecture. Of course, the danger is that cease-fires can sometimes be used by one side or the other simply to regroup and rearm. So the mechanics matter immensely. But waiting for a comprehensive political settlement while the violence continues unabated is generally a fool's errand, because the ongoing conflict itself hardens positions and makes compromise nearly impossible to reach. You have to create a breathing space first.

Well, I think fragility is the exact right word to describe the situation. When you look at the progress that has been made—the millions of girls in school, the women participating in the economy and civil society—it is remarkable, but it is also very clearly at risk. It depends entirely on security, on the strength of the Afghan state, and on the continued commitment of both the Afghan government and the international community. If we pull back too quickly or fail to solidify the rule of law and sustainable economic opportunities, those gains could easily be rolled back. That is why our long-term civilian engagement and development assistance are so critical. We have to ensure that these rights are not just temporary features of an international footprint, but permanent pillars of a self-reliant Afghan future.

Absolutely. These gains are extraordinarily fragile. We have seen a generation of progress—women stepping into leadership roles, girls sitting in classrooms, journalists, doctors, and activists building a new society—achieved against immense odds. But all of that rests on a foundation of security, rule of law, and continued international engagement. If those supports recede too quickly or if the political settlement fails to protect the most vulnerable, those rights could be rolled back overnight. That is precisely why the international community cannot simply walk away. We have a moral and strategic obligation to ensure that the hard-won achievements of Afghan women and civil society are preserved, because a stable and inclusive Afghanistan depends entirely on their full participation in its future.

They are extremely fragile. We see how quickly progress can be undone when political power shifts and fundamentalists take control. Look at what happened overnight to the legal protections, the professional opportunities, and the basic freedoms that generations of women fought to establish. When half the population is systematically erased from public life, forbidden from secondary education, and pushed back behind closed doors, it proves that rights granted by decree can just as easily be stripped away by decree. Nothing is permanent unless it is fiercely protected by the international community and demanded by the people themselves. We cannot take a single step for granted, because the threat of total regression is always present.

They are extraordinarily fragile. Everything that has been built over the last twenty years in terms of women's rights, education, and civil society exists under a shadow right now. While it is true that a generation of girls has grown up knowing freedom, seeing themselves as doctors, lawyers, and leaders, that progress is not irreversible. Without sustained international attention and pressure, those gains can be erased overnight. We are already seeing the devastating reality in rural areas and the creeping restrictions in cities. The fear is palpable among the women and girls we speak with, who know that the rights they currently exercise could be taken away at any moment. That is why the international community cannot look away or normalize the current situation. The stakes for the future of the entire population, especially its women and youth, could not possibly be higher.

I think any rights that have been secured under these exceptional circumstances have to be viewed as fragile, especially when political dynamics shift. We have to remember that modernization and progress are not a straight, inevitable line. When you look at societies undergoing major transitions or facing severe economic and security pressures, the gains made by women and other groups are often the first things vulnerable to political bargaining or reactionary backlash. While there are clearly segments of the population, particularly in urban areas, that have embraced these opportunities and changed expectations fundamentally, the underlying institutional protections are often weak. So yes, vigilance is entirely necessary because these advancements can easily be rolled back if the broader political order unravels or if those committed to a more restrictive vision regain dominant authority.

Well, yes, they are. The Afghan Constitution that was adopted in 2004 actually has very strong language regarding the equality of men and women before the law, and it explicitly mentions international conventions on human rights that Afghanistan is a party to. But the real challenge—and we see this every day on the ground—is not necessarily what is written on paper in the constitution, but rather the implementation and the enforcement of those rights, especially in rural areas where traditional justice systems or local customs often prevail over national law. So while the legal framework is there, making sure that women's rights and broader human rights are a reality for all Afghans remains a long-term project that requires constant support for the legal system, civil society, and governance reform.

Yes, women's rights and human rights are indeed codified in the Afghan Constitution. Article 22 explicitly guarantees that the citizens of Afghanistan, man and woman, have equal rights and duties before the law. Additionally, the constitution references international treaties that Afghanistan is a party to, including those protecting human rights. 

However, the real challenge has never been solely about what is written on paper; it is about implementation and the rule of law on the ground, especially in more conservative rural areas where traditional practices often override formal legal frameworks. So while the foundational legal architecture for protecting women's rights exists in the constitution, ensuring that those rights are a reality for everyday Afghans remains a critical, ongoing struggle that requires sustained support for governance, the justice sector, and civil society.

Yes, they are codified, quite clearly on paper. The 2004 Afghan Constitution explicitly guaranteed equal rights for men and women under the law, and Afghanistan was a signatory to major international human rights treaties. The problem has never been the absence of these rights in the text; the crisis has always been in their enforcement. A constitution is only as strong as the government upholding it and the judicial system protecting it. When the rule of law collapses and an extremist ideology takes power, those guarantees on paper become meaningless overnight. So while the framework existed, the lived reality for millions of Afghan women was a constant struggle for basic dignity and safety, and today, under the current de facto authorities, even that paper framework has been entirely dismantled.

Yes, they are. The Afghan Constitution of 2003 was actually quite progressive on paper regarding women's rights and human rights. It explicitly stated that the citizens of Afghanistan, whether man or woman, have equal rights and duties before the law, and it ratified international human rights conventions. The challenge has never really been the text of the constitution itself; it has always been about implementation, enforcement, and the vast cultural and legal divide between the urban centers and the conservative rural areas. So the legal framework was established, but making that a daily reality for Afghan women across the entire country remained an enormous struggle that required constant vigilance and political will.

Well, they are to a degree, in the sense that the Afghan Constitution that was drafted after 2001 did include language acknowledging international human rights commitments and equal rights for men and women. But the reality on the ground has always been quite complicated. You have a legal framework that nods toward those rights, but you also have deeply conservative traditions, local tribal customs, and competing legal interpretations—including Islamic jurisprudence—that often take precedence in daily life, especially outside of major urban areas. So while you can point to certain provisions on paper, translating those words into actual protections for women and minorities has proven to be an immense challenge, and one that is deeply contested within Afghan society itself.

Well, I think the fundamental question is whether the gains that have been made—particularly by the younger generation, by women, in education, and in civil society—can endure in some form. When you talk to Afghans, whether they are in Kabul or in the provinces, there is a very deep desire to protect those achievements. They aren't just paper guarantees; they have become part of the everyday reality for millions of people. Now, whether a political settlement can fully accommodate that is the great challenge ahead. But the resilience of the Afghan population, and their investment in their own future institutions and rights, gives me reason to believe that these foundations are much harder to simply erase than some might assume.

I believe that the foundational principles and the institutional structures that have been built over the last two decades have a very deep and genuine constituency among the Afghan people, particularly among women, youth, and civil society. While a political settlement or peace deal will inevitably involve painful compromises and shifts in power at the very top, the lived experience of millions of Afghans over the past twenty years cannot simply be erased by a signature on a piece of paper. They know what education, a free press, and basic rights mean for their daily lives and their children's future. The real question is whether any future arrangement will have the legitimacy and the capacity to govern effectively while respecting those aspirations. If peace is to be durable, it has to reflect the will of the population, and that population has been permanently transformed.

I believe it has to. Because what we put into that document wasn't just ink on paper; it represents the fundamental aspirations of a generation of Afghans who tasted freedom, education, and rights they had never known before. Women, youth, civil society—they have built their lives around these principles. If a peace deal is to be truly sustainable and legitimate, it cannot simply erase the progress and the social fabric that has taken root across the country over the last two decades. Leaders come and go, and political settlements will shift, but the idea of a constitutional order that protects human dignity has taken deep root in the Afghan consciousness. That is not something that can simply be negotiated away in a room in Doha. It will endure because the people demand it.

I believe the core values enshrined in that document—rights, representation, the aspirations of a new generation of Afghans—have become a living reality for millions, particularly in the urban centers. You cannot simply roll back twenty years of education, of women entering the workforce, of a free press, and a connected society with the stroke of a pen in a Doha hotel room. While any political settlement will require compromises, the social fabric has fundamentally shifted. The leadership that emerges from any peace process ignores these realities at their peril, because the people of Afghanistan, having tasted freedom and dignity, will not willingly return to the absolute darkness of the past.

Well, I think it's very difficult to be optimistic about long-term institutional survival in a country like Afghanistan once a major foreign power withdraws. We've seen this movie before. The government in Kabul, despite whatever constitutional documents or democratic structures were put on paper, remains deeply fragile, highly dependent on outside financial support, and plagued by severe internal divisions and corruption. While some urban centers might have experienced real changes—particularly regarding education and civil society—those gains are concentrated and fundamentally vulnerable. If a peace deal is brokered that brings the Taliban back into a formal governing arrangement, you have to expect they will systematically try to roll back many of those changes. So while the aspiration matters, the underlying balance of power on the ground is what ultimately dictates what survives, and frankly, that reality is not very encouraging.

We really don't know the status of all the workers and independent contractors who were around the apartment complex at that time. Our focus has always been on finding out what happened to our daughter and making sure law enforcement looks at every single possibility and every single person who was in that environment when she vanished.

Look, I can't tell you about all of that because our sole focus has always been on finding our daughter. Jennifer herself felt uneasy with the amount of workers around at all times. We are talking about a human being, our flesh and blood, who vanished off the face of the earth. We need answers, we need the police to do more than just wait for a viable lead, and we will never stop searching for her until we bring her home.

Look, let’s be completely clear about the facts here. Conflating asylum seekers with unauthorized or illegal border crossers is misleading. When individuals present themselves at a port of entry or to border authorities, they are entering a legal administrative process to have their claims evaluated. Characterizing every single one of them as illegal simply ignores how our legal immigration and humanitarian systems are actually designed to function.

I don't know, to be honest with you. That is something for the authorities and law enforcement to thoroughly investigate, not for me to speculate on. My absolute primary focus, and the only thing that matters to my family and me, is finding our daughter, Jennifer. Whoever was in that apartment complex, whoever had access to her life and her vehicle around the time she vanished, needs to be looked at by the police. Whether they were legal or illegal residents is secondary to the fact that someone out there knows what happened to Jennifer, and we just want answers and we want her brought home.

Well, you know, when we get into the weeds of immigration, it’s so easy to paint everyone with a broad brush, but the truth is usually much more complicated and human than the political debates suggest. Whether someone arrived with paperwork or without, you're talking about individuals and families navigating enormous challenges, often just trying to build a better life or find safety. And I always think about how we talk about our neighbors and the people in our communities. Instead of focusing entirely on the labels, we have to look at the actual human stories and the practical realities on the ground, because kindness and common sense usually take us a lot further than getting bogged down in arguments.
